source.title: Agents Are All You Need for LLM Unlearning

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices and tables; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports attack results that support vulnerability of some post-hoc methods but challenge the broad claim that prompting attacks recover information from every unlearning method: ALU is reported as robust in the tested settings, with some model- and attack-specific qualifications.
record.gate_note: The paper tests target masking, jailbreak prompts, translations into other languages, and many-shot jailbreaking against ICUL, Guardrail, and ALU. It also reports WMDP accuracy for ALU and comparison methods. The displayed Table 3 None-perturbation scores are used as baselines below, not duplicated as attack rows. The Harry Potter response examples in Appendix A.8 are qualitative examples and are not additional rows where the corresponding attack condition is already represented in Table 3.
record.test_reason: The study runs prompt-only attacks (target masking, jailbreak prefixes, translation, 128-shot jailbreaking) against inference-time unlearning methods (ICUL, Guardrail) and reports leakage via GPT privacy scores. It also proposes ALU, a new method claimed robust to these attacks (version F). The setting is new because the methods are post-hoc filters, not weight edits. No fine-tuning, activation or quantization attacks are run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim no indirect leakage for ALU in any setting. They attribute ALU's jailbreak score drops to conservative 'I don't know' responses rather than leakage.
record.recipe_differences: ALU is a multi-agent, inference-time response-filtering framework; it does not update weights or use the original weight-unlearning recipes. It is compared with cited unlearning methods and post-hoc baselines rather than reproducing the original studies' attack protocols in full.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with base model size/model, attack type, and language; ALU shows lower scores under jailbreak prompts, and Llama-3.2 3B has translation-related performance drops.

fits_no_version.finding: Information leakage rises with target-set sparsity (1000 targets, 2% real). NPO leaks nearly all 20 targets at 980:20; ALU leaks little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning leaks targets when they are buried among many dummy forget targets.

record.problems: The prompt-attack evaluation uses a limited controlled set of Harry Potter questions; each question was evaluated thrice and the best score was used, then means were reported. GPT-4o is used as the privacy-score judge. The paper does not define the numeric score direction or scale in the Table 3 presentation, although it supplies qualitative interpretations. The ALU WMDP evaluation modifies the framework to choose a random option after target detection, so it does not establish removal from weights. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 None-perturbation baseline values are included only in the baseline fields of attack rows. The 31-model WMDP accuracy results in Table 32 are not extracted individually; Table 1's ALU WMDP results and retained MMLU result were retained as the primary directly relevant accuracy evidence. Other model/dataset similarity and ROUGE comparisons were omitted because they do not test recovery attacks named in the versions.

untested.parts: Robustness of weight-based unlearning methods (RMU etc.) to attacks; whether knowledge is removed from weights.
Not tested: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Not tested: no activation ablation or internal analysis.
Prompt attacks on weight-unlearned models (only post-hoc methods are attacked); in-context-information attacks other than many-shot.
ALU's resistance to fine-tuning, internal-edit, quantization or white-box attacks. The authors assume black-box access.

missing.what: Guardrail and ALU WMDP accuracy on 31 models: Guardrail often far from chance (e.g. Llama-3-70B Bio 77.8), ALU ≤28 everywhere
Adversarial robustness scores for GA, NPO, WHP and others, scaled 20→100 targets, on WPU

record.verdict_notes: Versions remapped V1→A, V5→E, V6→F. Higher GPT privacy score means less target reference. The paper describes the score as 1–5, but Table 3 values reach 9.5, an unexplained scale. Each score is the best of three runs over three questions. ICUL and ALU are post-hoc filters, so E evidence here concerns inference-time 'unlearning', not weight unlearning. ALU rows are linked to F only, to avoid state conflicts with E.

versions.untested_parts: No direct test of whether the targeted knowledge was removed from model weights; ALU is inference-time. The paper does not test all methods named in the claim, nor recovery attacks based on fine-tuning, internal activation edits, quantization, or ordinary prompt rephrasing.
No fine-tuning or other relearning attack on unlearned models.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing whether the methods block access rather than delete knowledge.
Tests target masking, jailbreak prompts, other-language prompts, and many-shot jailbreaking; does not test fine-tuning, quantization, or ordinary paraphrase-only prompts as recovery attacks.
Tests ALU against the listed prompt perturbations and jailbreaks, not against fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or every attack named in the claim.
